utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At the beginning of your evidence you made a solemn declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. That declaration continues to apply to your evidence this morning, and you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, we won't have any questions for this witness. We've consulted with other Defence attorneys over the weekend and no questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic? Do you have any questions or Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I shall have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm Djuro Cepic, Defence counsel for General Lazarevic, and together with Mr. Bakrac and Mr. Milos Cvijic, we are the Defence team of General Vladimir Lazarevic in this courtroom. You made a statement on the 21st of October 2001, and on page 4 of the B/C/S version, English is page 4, last paragraph, and the Albanian version is page 5, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down with your question by the interpreters; if you could just speak a little more slowly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You stated that when you were just before Djakovica, you saw that the entire town was in flames. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the neighbourhood where I was going through. It was in the direction of the centre, because the police would not allow us to go towards the outskirts, and I saw that, the buildings there were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that it would not have been safe to go through a part of town that was in flames; is that not a logical conclusion?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was the police that told us to go in that direction. I don't know the town well. The police gave us a direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the following paragraph, you say that you know that there were girls from that village or from other villages that were taken out and raped. You are not a witness to that. You just heard about it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move back to the 26th of March 1999, that is referred to in several different places. You also referred to it in your own testimony before this Trial Chamber. Do you know that on that day, around 1600 hours, or to be more precise around 1630 hours in the village of Likovac, the following persons got killed, a policeman, or rather policemen in the plural, Milan Pavlovic, Dusan Trifunovic, Ljubovir Zivkovic, Dragivoj Gajic, and Radisa Krikovic [phoen], and that several of them were seriously wounded. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. They live in a different area from where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the 1st of April 1999, in the village of Bracina [phoen], that is also near your village, policeman Rasevic [phoen] was killed and two other policemen were seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the name of the village. What was the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Brocna [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no village with that name close to my village or around my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Give me just a minute to find the name of that village in the Albania language, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Broje [phoen] is the name of the village in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that case, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in that village, or rather in that region, there were two big brigades of the so-called KLA? Namely the 101st [as interpreted] in Srbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript, page 4, line 2, I said the 111th Brigade. I didn't say the 101st Brigade. I said the 111th. Okay. Thank you. Then the 113th Brigade in the village of Likovac. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Broje there was no such brigade as you mentioned, 111th, because the police were there, stationed there. I don't know whether they were anywhere else but I don't know that they were in Broje.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I mentioned Srbica, not Broje, as far as the so-called KLA was concerned, the 111th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's possible that a brigade existed in Skenderaj at that time. I don't believe that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are you knowledgeable about military formations generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: HADIJE FAZLIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just what I heard through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nothing from me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fazliu that brings your evidence to an end. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is Abdullah Salihu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if I can ask you at this stage to assist me in one respect in this, in relation to this witness. The statement that we have been given starts with references to events in 1998. Can you direct me to the part of the indictment that relates to these?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was having difficulty matching dates and places in the statement to the specific averments about 1998 in the indictment and I was hoping you could clarify that for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think his evidence regarding 1998 was not tied to a specific incident but rather related to, I think, paragraph 96 which talked about from approximately February 1998 until May 1998, or approximately 15.000 Kosovo Albanians with fled. Then by mid-October, United Nations estimated that approximately 285.000 persons had been internally displaced within the province. There was not a specific reference to his municipality or those 20.000 that he refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I note in fact, Mr. Hannis, the figure in the statement is 200.000. Is that a misprint?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he made a correction to that in his testimony in Milosevic that it should be 20.000 instead of 200.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Salihu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which is to be placed in front of you just now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Now, Mr. Salihu, we have already in front of us a statement and a transcript of evidence you gave before, so we have quite a lot of information already about the evidence you can give. At this stage in the proceedings, is to give the counsel representing the Prosecution and also representing the various accused in this case the opportunity to ask you further questions. These may be to clarify your evidence or to expand upon it and also to challenge it because it's part of the process under which these proceedings are conducted that counsel have an opportunity also to challenge you about the evidence, so don't be surprised if you're asked some questions which challenge what you've said. The first counsel to pose questions will be on behalf of the Prosecution, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Salihu. Would you state your name for us, please? Your full name.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Abdullah Salihu.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from your statement, Mr. Salihu, I understand that you were born and lived all your life in the village of Baks, in Skenderaj or Srbica municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to start with I'd like to show you a copy of your statement which is Exhibit P2255. And if I may hand a hard copy to the witness. And sir I would ask to you take a look at that and let us know if you recognise that as a statement you gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear your answer. Could you repeat that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: It's okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you confirm to the Court now that that is correct and is your evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I know previously when you testified in the Milosevic case you did make -- you pointed out one correction on the first page where you talked about the number of people gathered in the area of Cicavica in your written statement it was listed as 200.000 but that number is not correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. The number was 20.000, so it has to be 20.000 instead of 200.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We would like to tender that at this time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it simply the statement or are you tendering the transcript as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be useful to tender the transcript as well. I'm not sure of the -- may I consult for a moment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I apologise. I'm sorry, we had intended to proceed with this as an 89(F) statement based on his written statement only and not his prior transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I understood was the position but -- so we'll note that this is now part of the process, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, how big was your village in 1998? How many houses, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Before 1998, our village had about 130, 140 households.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know approximately how many people lived in those houses?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: About 2.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of the villagers?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see from your statement that you were the hodja?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what do you do in that job?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: An hodja is a cleric. He leads the people. He is a Muslim cleric. In Kosovo, there are Muslims, Catholics, Orthodox people but I am a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your statement you describe the events of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the Cicavica area is related to your village of Baks?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: The Cicavica area is about three kilometres from my village, to the east of the village where I live. There are several villages around that area, Kozica, Kasniaus [phoen], Kasalic [phoen], and other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you describe how it came to be that most of your villagers left the area and were living in the mountains, in the forest. At the top of page 3 of the English, you mention that about 80 per cent of the people had no place to stay and international organisations provided some basic aid like plastic covering. What international organisations were helping you at that time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. There were international organisations, Caritas was one. There was an organisation from Switzerland. There were several organisations that helped. They brought food, flour, they brought material to cover the roofs of the houses because they were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there any KLA presence in your village in the fall of 1998 through the spring of 1999?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: There were nine members from our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were they staying in the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: They stayed close to the village, not in the village. They had guard duty. They did guard duty. They just guarded the village. They stayed in various houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the spring of 1999, you mention that the OSCE --

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- left the area. Do you recall how long before the NATO bombings started that they left the area?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly but two or three months before that. It was after the OSCE left that the people all got weapons, got armed, especially in the municipality where I lived, and in Qires. People got weapons and we had to go to the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say people all got weapons, especially in the municipality where you lived, which people are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your previous answer, you said --

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I meant the Serbian army. They came with weapons, tanks, APCs, trucks, and they came to the municipality of Qires. There were buses, there were paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. In your statement in the second paragraph in the English on page 3, you mention that the paramilitaries came. Can you describe what you define as paramilitaries, versus, for example, the regular army, the VJ, or the police? How did these paramilitaries look different, if they did?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. They were different. During the whole time, until the war ended, I saw three kinds of clothes, I can call them, they were wearing. One of them was the regular uniform. I had been before a member of the Yugoslavian army, a long time ago. I had seen that uniform. Normally, the normal soldiers are young in age, while the paramilitaries, they were 35 years old, 40 years old, even 50 years old, and they had long hair and beards and they had painted faces, bandanas around their heads. And part of them were reservists, because when we were held hostage in the village of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Close to Kamarana [phoen] and they explained to us that the army has forcefully recruited us and told us to come and fight in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you a couple of questions. Could you repeat the name of the village where you were held by the reservists?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Vukovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there any way you could distinguish what you described as the reservist from paramilitaries? Or are you talking about VJ reservist?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. The reservists had the same uniform. It was kind of grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The same kind of uniform as the regular VJ?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm confused. Can you explain for me the difference between the regular VJ, full-time VJ, the professional VJ, on the one hand, the reservists you've told us about, and paramilitaries, three different kinds of groups?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. The Yugoslav army, the regular army, had a uniform that had three colours, camouflage green and grey and yellow. The paramilitary had the same uniform but they had long beards, long hair. They had bandanas and they had armed bands, red, blue, yellow. Reservists had grey uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I understand much better now. Now, in your statement, you mentioned that after the OSCE left and paramilitaries came into your area, that you, you and the other villagers sought shelter in the forest. Near the middle of page 3 of the English you indicate on the 28th of April --

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- NATO attacked the Feronikel factories in Gllogoc. First of all, can you tell us how you were aware of that? Did you actually see it yourself?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were the Feronikel factories? Do you know what they made there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: The Feronikel factory, it was a factory where they processed nickel, smelt nickel, from the nickel ore. But after the Serbs expelled the workers from the factory, it was used as a kind of a barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: After the workers were expelled, before the war started, so the workers were expelled, were fired from their jobs, and the Serbian army and the Serbian paramilitaries used that factory as their barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You describe in your statement how the day after that happened, that on the 29th of April, you and a small group of men were captured in the area you describe as Fush e Molles. F-u-s-h and then the single letter e and then M-o-l-l-e-s. What is that? Is that a river, a mountain, a village? What is Fush e Molles?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: This place, it's a mountain, it's -- on one side there is a mountain and on the other there is a hill and there is a field in between. And that's what it's called Fush e Molles, which means "the apple field." It is between Vrboc [phoen], Baks, Qires, Dushets [phoen], Likoshan, Novo Sel [phoen]. I've got a map here if I can help you with that map to see where these places are, to see more clearly where these places are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have -- I have a map we'll put it up and ask you to take a look at it and see if you can show us where some of these places are. If we could have P615? And I believe it's at page 18. This is the Kosovo atlas. And Mr. Salihu, hopefully you'll have a map up on your screen in a minute. Could we go to about the middle of the page? Yes. That's good. I don't know if you can see on there, Mr. Salihu, do you see your village of Baks?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. There it is, Baks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there is a pen that the usher has there which you can use to actually touch the screen and draw on the screen. If you would, could you draw a circle around your village? Just draw a small circle.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: This is where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you also draw a circle around Qires? And I believe you described there was a triangle formed by those two villages and a third village called Vrboc?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could draw a circle around it as well?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I can't see Vrboc here. Must be here somewhere but I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell from my view but if you would look directly south of Baks and to the left, is that the village you're talking about? I can't read the printing quite that well but it seems to --

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, there it is, Vrboc is here and also Stutica, Dushets, Likoshan, Glanasella, and this part here is Fush e Molles. Skatova [phoen], here it is here, while we were here, in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put a little X with a circle around it to show the approximate location where you were captured?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one of these that would not be clear I suspect, Mr. Hannis, would be Fush e Molles, which doesn't have that name in the circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see your point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could we actually have read out what is in the circle that represents Fush e Molles?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you understand that, Mr. Salihu? When you mentioned Fush e Molles, you drew a circle around something that on the map has a different name. Could you read us that name where you indicated Fush e Molles is, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Fush e Molles is here between these two villages, in the middle, where the X is. That's what is called Fush e Molles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I understand now, thank you. Could we take a screen shot of that and give it the next IC exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit IC 13, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Salihu, you tell us in your statement about how you were captured and what happened to you and the other men. How you were eventually taken with a bigger group and went to the mosque in Qires, and you detail what happened to you and the other men there. You state in your statement, at the top of page 5 in the English version, that the mosque was burned from a previous offensive. Was the roof still intact at that time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you an exhibit now, if we could. This is a photograph and it's Exhibit P1801. This will be coming up on your screen in a moment and I'll ask if you recognise what that is.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: This is the mosque of Qires village, where we were detained for one night after we were captured at the Fush e Molles. It was around 3 p.m. they brought us here. It's about three kilometres from the place where we were captured. When we came to the mosque, the mosque was burned. The windows, the doors, everything wooden had been burned. We were kept there for one night, and it was a Friday, it was the Friday night. Then the next day, on Saturday, when they took us to Gllogoc we went to a place about four kilometres close to Gllogoc called Shavarina. We were ill treated. We were beaten up --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before we --

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: -- in the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before we go to that I need to ask you another picture about the photograph. The night you were detained at the mosque on the 29th of April 29, 1999, did it look like it looks in that picture?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The walls were already down?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No, no, they weren't down yet. They were damaged about 15 days before the Serb forces withdrew from Kosovo. The mosque was burnt, the windows were gone, the doors, everything wooden was burnt. But the walls, the tile walls, brick walls, survived, and the minaret was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So did the damage that appears to the walls in this picture, did that occur then after you were there on the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. It was about the end of April. Or, no, in May, it was, rather, that it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you know about that damage that occurred later?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I heard about it because it was -- I knew about my village and the villages surrounding Cicavica. We were in -- under tents. It was, I think, the third day that they destroyed it, with mines, with bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: From my cousins, uncles, other people in the village. I did not see it myself when -- at the moment it was destroyed but I just heard that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during the time that were you detained there, I think you said that there were 176 of you. How do you know the precise number?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I know we were gathered in three groups. The first had about 50 people, the second about the same, and in the evening, we were all in the mosque in the evening, and they told us that the next morning we would all be shot if anyone is missing. So I know how many we were. We were 176. They counted us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now you describe in your statement how the next day a portion of you were put on three trucks and driven in the direction of Gllogoc and you went to a place you called -- is it Shiverina [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Shavarina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you describe in your statement the execution of a group of men from the first truck and then how a man arrived in a military jeep and had a conversation with the shooters or the man in charge. Can you describe that person who arrived in the jeep and spoke with the men who had been in charge of you and did the killing? Was he a paramilitary or a VJ or a policeman? Could you tell?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: When they brought us from Qires to Shavarina, as I said, there were three trucks of us there. The first truck, the people were taken out of the truck, were lined up, it was a big group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, the question is a very specific question and it would be helpful you could listen again to the question and answer the question that's actually being asked. Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, for the moment, I would just like to know if you can describe for us the person who arrived in the jeep after that group of men who were shot at the pit. Was he a paramilitary or a VJ or a policeman? What could you tell about him from his appearance?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: He wasn't a policeman. Nor was he a paramilitary. He was a member of the regular army. And he went -- I don't know what he said to them. I couldn't hear. But after he talked to them, to the group, the shooting stopped. Some of them, I think 30 people, were killed and the other two trucks were taken away to Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then in your statement --

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I don't know if that is clear what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And then in your statement, where you give some details about this, you mentioned that the two truckloads of you that were still alive were taken to Gllogoc, and you tell us what happened to you and your group. You were taken to the police station and then to the cinema building and how you were beaten. You mention the killing of one individual in your group named Rhaman Topilla. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I can remember. We were taken to Gllogoc and were beaten all day, chained to the wall with our hands behind our backs and around our heads. And on the third day, a paramilitary came from the train station, about 100 metres away, and talked to a policeman near us in Serbian. "Give me the people who belong to me." The paramilitary had raki in one hand and a rifle in the other, and they took Rahman Topilla away, ten metres away from us, and shot him there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions about that. Do you speak and understand Serbian?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say the paramilitary asked or said, "give me the people who belong to me." And then you say they took Rahman away. Who is "they" that took him ten metres away and shot him? Was it just one person or more than one person?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. It was just Rahman who was taken away and he was shot, and we stayed there for six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was how many people took Rahman away? Was it just one person who took him away or more than one person?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: It was just one. It was a Serb paramilitary, as I said, who came from the train station Gllogoc. He had an automatic rifle in one hand, raki in the other. It was only one. And he talked to the policeman and said, "Give me the person who belongs to me." And the policeman said, "Take whoever you want." And they -- he took Rahman away, about ten metres away from us, and shot him. It was only one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the policeman who spoke with him, can you describe him for us? What kind of uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: He had a normal police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you explain to me what you mean by a normal police uniform? We've heard testimony about different kinds of police uniforms. What do you mean by "normal"?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: It was blue, it was a bit mixed in colours, with some black.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So some police uniforms we've heard described as having plain or solid-colour blue and we've heard some described as camouflage.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. It was a camouflaged. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you tell us about your stay at the police station and being beaten and being questioned and that on the seventh day, trucks came and took you away to Vukovc, where you stayed until the end of the fighting in mid-June 1999. And you describe how you were treated by the VJ reserve where you were doing work by the open trenches, et cetera. Did you have any conversation with the VJ reserve who were in charge of you there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. We did. To tell you the truth, when they took us to Vukovc they gave us food when we were staying there because we hadn't had any food for eight days. They gave us cigarettes and treated us well, with the exception of four people who were paramilitaries in that group of reservists. The reservists treated us well. We were about 37 to 40 days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, in your statement you describe that the -- I'm sorry, was there --

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: And we did talk to them and they told us that we didn't come to liberate this region, we came to occupy it. We were forced to come here. We didn't want to. It's -- they said, "It's your country and we don't want to force you to dig ditches but we have to," and they gave us food. They said that they were forced to come there and fight against the Albanians. And I have respect for the people I talked to there. They -- as I said, the others treated us brutally but not there. Right until the end, we got along well with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I just have a couple more topics with you and then I'll be finished, Mr. Salihu. Do you suffer any long-term effects as a result of the beatings you suffered after you were captured?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I'm not the only one who suffered. I have four ribs -- had four ribs broken. My foot or my leg was injured. To put it briefly, when they sent me to the mosque to be executed, I would rather have been executed than to have survived all this, but thanks to NATO, thanks to God, things turned out well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last thing I want --

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: But I'm still suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last thing I want to ask you, if we could show you a map one more time. Again this is P615 at page 18. And on this map, Mr. Salihu, when it's up, I would like to ask if you can locate on there area where the shooting of the men from the truck took place. If we could go a little closer to Gllogoc, scroll down a bit. Okay, that's good. On that map, are you able to see the area where you saw the men executed? Where the pit was?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: It was here, in Chatova Vijetera [phoen]. That's the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement, you describe how the men were shot and fell over the edge of the pit. Did the shooters do anything after the men were shot and had fallen into the pit?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: When they shot them, they put them in three lines, and those who shot them, each one was responsible for one line, and after they were all shot, and they threw two or three grenades at them to make sure that no one survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, one other location on this map I'd like you to mark because Gllogoc is clearer to us but the location where you were taken and worked on the trenches with the reservists, I think you said Vukovc. Does that appear on this map?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. It's the road between Kamaran and Peja or Pristina-Peja, on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you draw us a circle or a box in that approximate area where that was, if you can tell?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I don't think it's here. You'd have to enlarge the map on one side, Drenac [phoen] the lower part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see the village of Kamaran [phoen] down there. Is that the village you mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: The village of Kamaran, yes, it's here, yeah, and it's right near -- yeah, there is Vukovc in the valley of Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have a screen shot of that and give it the next IC exhibit number? And then I have no other questions for you at this time, Mr. Salihu. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number IC 14, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions. We will proceed in this order: General Pavkovic, Mr. Sainovic, General Lukic, General Lazarevic, and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. At the very beginning I'm going to want to have P1801 re-displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Salihu, good morning, my name is John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic in this proceeding. I have a -- very few questions I'm going to ask you. We'll get through this very quickly if you just answer precisely the questions I ask you, we will be finished in a very, very short period of time, okay?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: What I said in my statement, you can ask me anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us during your testimony here today, if I remember it properly, that there were approximately 176 of you who were captured at this Fush e Molles place. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that's what he said as far as the captured. That was the number in the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you got to this mosque at Qires that you should be able to see on your screen right now, do you see it?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that 176 people spent the night in that building?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I now want to ask you just very briefly about that incident you described where a paramilitary came with a -- with raki in one hand and a gun in the other and asked for somebody and killed him. I just want to clarify a matter, when you say "raki" or the transcript says "raki" you're referring to alcohol, liquor, a bottle of liquor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I now want to talk to you very briefly about some testimony you gave in the Milosevic case. You told the Chamber in the Milosevic case that you now regret not being a member of the KLA. Does that remain your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a page reference, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I would just like to explain something, though. If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you want to explain something that would be up to the Prosecutor to ask you perhaps or -- I think you've answered my question, that that remains your position. You also told the Milosevic Chamber that the KLA was not dangerous. Those are your words, "not dangerous." 4613. You said, "I know that the KLA defended the people as much as they could and were capable of." So I take it it's your position that the KLA was a peace-loving organisation simply defending the people. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your view, they were not a group of dangerous rebels seeking to create an independent state of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: They were not rebels or extremists. They were people helping the poor population, the population, they did what they could to help people, old people, children, to help the suffering population. They were not paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that the KLA was a military organisation rebelling against the government of Serbia and killing people in the process, seeking independence for Kosovo? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No, that's not true. They didn't kill people. They didn't go to Serbia to attack people and kill them there. It was the Serbs who came to our country to attack us, to expel us from our houses, to kill. You can't change history around. They didn't -- we didn't do it in their country. They did it in our country. They came to Kosova. They expelled us from our own country, over a million people. We were forced to leave Kosovo. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, you can't change history either. Kosovo was not a country. Kosovo was a province of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that a question or a speech?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not a speech. It's a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Kosovo was part of Serbia, wasn't it? They didn't come to your country, they came to their country. It was part of Serbia. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No, that's not true. I never had my house in Serbia. I had my home in the village of Baks. I wasn't sent to Belgrade. It was the people from Belgrade who came and expelled me from my house. It was never a part of Serbia and never will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The name Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, it stands for Kosovo Liberation Army, doesn't it? That's what those letters mean. Not Kosovo Defence Army. Right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: The president of Kosova, Mr. Ibrahim Rugova, explained that very well. It was a group of people protecting their own houses, their own homes, and they called it the Kosovo Liberation Army. I can't tell you any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just have one more question for you. I want to know that, if in giving your testimony here today and in the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor you had the same regard for the truth as the testimony you have given about the character of the KLA. Did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's an impossible question to answer, Mr. Ackerman. It's a comment, really, and that will be better made at the appropriate time, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That ends my questioning then, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in actual fact I only have one question that is actually aimed at clarifying a particular term and that will be useful to all, won't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sir, on page 3, the one-but-last paragraph in the B/C/S -- will you understand me if I speak to you in B/C/S? I mean, in Serbian? You said that this paramilitary group that had surrounded you and taken you prisoner had a Seselj emblem on their right sleeves. What is this Seselj emblem?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please describe this for us?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: It was smaller than this here, metallic, and it said, "Seselj grupa" or "militarska grupa." [Realtime transcript read in error, "Q."] That is how they were calling out to each other? I saw that with my own eyes during the 40 days I was with them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note it was all the answer but in two languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: There is problem in transcript. Page 27, paragraph 3 is line -- is a question, that's how they were calling out to each other. I think that was answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, you're saying that the whole of 27, line 1 to 4 is an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That no doubt will be corrected in the final version of the transcript. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In conclusion, so you saw this metal badge where it said Seselj's army or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No. It wasn't written on the badges. There was an eagle, when they were called into action they were called, "Hey, come on, Seselj's group, military group." In Serbian. That's how they called them. It was a metal badge, metallic badge with an eagle and the flag of Yugoslavia on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you understood their conversation to mean that it was Seselj's group?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. So these are the people with whom you spent 40 days? 40 days, you said that you spent 40 days with them?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, I was among them for 40 days, or about 37 to be exact, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. When you said that they stole 600 deutschmark from you and your documents, you said that the Serbs simply threw them away. Now, who are these Serbs? Are they Seselj's men or some other Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: They were Seselj's people, they were Seselj's people there. There were paramilitaries there and other groups, three different types were there. When we were taken prisoner in Fush e Molles I had 600 deutschmark in my pocket and tobacco, and a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify something. You use this word "Serbs." It was 8 million of Serbs, 8 million Serbs, and I'm one of them. And in your statement the say, "the Serbs threw away my documents." You do not say paramilitaries. Do you understand? That is the clarification I sought. I'm trying to explain to you what it was that I was asking you about, and I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I called the paramilitaries Serbs. It's -- you can write paramilitary, normal army but they were all Serbs, weren't they? Were they not Serbs? Sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But there are Serbs who are not members of paramilitary formations, right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: But all those who were --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I know, all of these who were paramilitaries were Serbs. I understood that so that is the clarification I sought.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: All of those who came to Kosova were Serbs. They were paramilitaries, normal army members, and Seselj's army in the place which I called Fush e Molles. And they took 600 marks, they took my watch, they took my cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Salihu. I'm Branko Lukic, together with Mr. Ivetic and Mr. Ogrizovic, I am Defence counsel for General Lukic before this Tribunal. I will have a few questions related to your statement as well as to your testimony before this Tribunal in the Milosevic trial. But I would like to start with what you were talking about today. On page 9, line 8, you referred to the area of Cicavica. Your own village and the villages that you marked today, do they all belong to that area?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: The villages I mentioned around Fush e Molles, there are four villages, from the municipality of Skenderaj and four from the village of Drajnoc [phoen]. They were all around Cicavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 9, line 23, you talked about nine members of the KLA. Did those people live in your village while they were members of the KLA? Did they sleep there in that village?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: They -- yes, they lived with the population. They were part of the population and lived and slept there. But they couldn't stay there during the offensive of Cicavica but they -- no one was there during the fighting but they had lived there for 30 years beforehand because they had all been expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to the fighting later. On page 12, line 23, you refer to the Feronikel factory. Were all the workers laid off, all the workers of that factory?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So regardless of their ethnic background, because the factory simply went out of operation, right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: The factory was closed because of the enforced measures introduced by Serbia. That's why it was closed. I know that. I know very well what was going on in Kosova before the war. There were all these imposed measures from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is a normal police uniform, as far as you're concerned? Please tell me.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I can describe it quite easily. Normal police -- I mean as long as the Albanians were in the police there. But when the Albanians were expelled from the police force, the uniforms were changed. They were blue and then later they were camouflaged. They were sort of bluish camouflage colours. I don't know who was responsible for expelling the policemen from the police force. Perhaps you could explain that to me? Who expelled the Albanians from the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot explain anything to you from here but you are supposed to give explanations to me. Is it correct that Albanian policemen left the police force and that Serbia tried to keep the ethnic Albanian policemen on the force but that they refused to do so? And we heard testimony about that before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a compound question and we don't have a time period that we are talking about. And is he asking him to agree that we had testimony about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, do you know that ethnic Albanian policemen in Kosovo left the police force after 1989?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. From what I've heard, I saw what happened on television. They were forcefully expelled. They did not leave the police force of their own free will. In my statement, I refer to a policeman. He was a civilian, U-d-b-a, and he tried to help the Albanians and help me, Momir Piljevic. I think now he lives somewhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about that. I would like to ask you on what TV was it that you saw and heard that ethnic Albanian policemen were expelled from the police force. Can you also give us a date or at least an approximate date?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: The whole world heard about it. I can't give you any specific details. I don't know the date but the whole world heard about it. It was reported on the BBC, on the Voice of America, in a lot of stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, it's a matter for you whether you wish to go down this particular road which seems to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Been directed by a question that was rightfully identified should not have been asked of you. But we are departing from what this evidence is mainly about. It's a matter for you, of course. You're entitled to do so but I wonder if we are going to be assisted by this witness's evidence on the matters that you're asking at the moment. However, you can reflect on that and we'll resume in 20 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salihu, I would kindly ask you to provide as brief answers to my questions as possible. If we may need a clarification, it can be asked of you by the Chamber or perhaps later on by the Prosecutor, and I'm doing this in order to save time and to go through your statement as quickly as possible. On page 21, line 5, you said you were digging trenches. Were you able to carry out that work the same way the other people who were digging alongside you were?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody was digging trenches. We were -- there were 16 of us in the same place, a group of 16, and we were asked to do the same thing. We all worked the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the four broken ribs did not bother you and you said your leg was hurt as well but nevertheless you were digging trenches as well as the other people and you said you had sustained those injuries immediately before that.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: It is true, and I can show you my ribs, and the injury in my leg, but I have to tell you that we worked as much as we could. The army behaved very well towards us at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether anyone from your village was killed as a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No. They were there to help the people, not to kill them. No, nobody killed anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you if you knew whether anyone from your village was killed as a member of the KLA, fighting for the KLA.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. By the Serbian army. Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You probably know that in the fall of 1998, the Kosovo Verification Mission arrived, headed by Mr. William Walker. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph -- on page 3 of the English and paragraph 1, and page 3, paragraph 1 of the Albanian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In the Albanian page 3, paragraph 3, and in the B/C/S page 3, paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- you say in the winter of 1998 and 1999 you say, "we were in constant fear because there was shelling every day." Do you believe we can reconfirm that if we went through the Kosovo Verification Mission reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, how do you think -- how do you think this witness will answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the area where you lived, did you used to see any Kosovo Verification Mission members?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were some, and they were welcome because we thought we were going to be liberated. We felt as if we were liberated when we saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Serb forces were unable to conduct any activities unless they had previously notified the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I did not ask any of those verification missions what they did. However, they -- the Serbian forces did not care whether the verification mission was there or not because villages, some villages away from where the mission was, they did what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you believe that there were actions undertaken by Serb forces without the prior knowledge of the Kosovo Verification Mission? Is that what you're stating today?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in the Cicavica area, the 114th Brigade was active, the 114th Brigade of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. I know. I did know. It was not called a brigade. I think you're wrong in calling it a brigade. I think it was called Group 14, because every four or five villages, they got together and they tried to protect -- some people tried to protect that part of the population in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Samir Lushtaku, Beqim Jashari [phoen], and Nuredin Lushtaku, do these names mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I know Sami Lushtaku. He's a friend. Nuredin Lushtaku, I -- he's just an acquaintance. Sami Beqiri [phoen], I'm not sure about the name. I don't think I know this person, Sami Beqiri. It's not Samir, it's Sami Lushtaku.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Precisely, sir, Sami Lushtaku?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that he commanded the 114th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. No, he wasn't a commander. I don't think you have the right information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we please show D -- 6 D67 to the witness? Page 27. But first of all, let us see the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is 6 D67.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have it in both English and Albanian but we were unfortunately unable to locate the Albanian text since this -- these are newspaper articles. Therefore, the paragraph numbering does not correspond between the statements. On page 1, it is stated that this is an interview conducted with Sulejman Salimi [phoen] [Previous translation continues] [In English] ... "army commander and current Kosova Protection Force deputy commander." [Interpretation] Therefore, we have an interview here with one of the leaders of the KLA. At page 27, the last paragraph, I will read it out in English so that you would receive appropriate interpretation. [In English] "The units of all the brigades around took part in the attack that was carried out against the Serbs, Serb forces, that started from Skenderaj. A unit of 114 Brigade led by Sami Lushtaku, Beqim Jashari, and Nuredin Lushtaku took part in the attack in Prekaz and in the first wars of Skenderaj." [Interpretation] Mr. Salihu?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I don't understand this very well. Did they fight in Prekaz or where?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here, the fighting in Prekaz is mentioned but judging by this part of the statement by a high official of the KLA, it becomes clear that Sami Lushtaku as well as Beqir Jashari and Nuredin Lushtaku led or commanded the 114th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not correct, Your Honour. It says, "a unit of the 114th."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Hannis, this doesn't say that he's the leader of the 114th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A unit that was part of the 114th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've started off on the wrong leg. It's difficult to get back on to the right one after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm standing on one leg, Your Honour, that's why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you read to me, you can ask the right person. I'm not the right person to ask me this question. I have made a statement. I have given here an account of what I've seen and what I have heard but I don't know what answer to give to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I accept your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps it can be clarified to some extent. You said that, Mr. Salihu, that you knew Sami Lushtaku.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you know him to be a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did you know whether he led a part of the 114th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what part he led or whether he led a part. As I said, there were people who got together to protect the population but I don't know who was leading. I wasn't part of that group so I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the next page, page 28, the first paragraph, since you also mentioned the Feronikel factory --

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the second sentence, the text reads as follows, and yet again I will read in English to reduce the number of languages used. [In English] "The shelling of the villages around Cicavica started from the Feronikel factory. Our soldiers resisted continuously but the huge Serb forces managed to advance from Oshlan, close to Qires, on the third day. They managed to advance to Qires only on the fourth day of the attack." Therefore, Mr. Salihu, can we see from this that the KLA was not exactly an organisation which dealt only in humanitarian activities but it participated actively in fighting the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No. That's not true. They did not have the weapons, the armament to fight. They were with the people, with the population, to the last day. They might have had only a Kalashnikov or light weapons. They did not have any tanks or heavy weaponry. They just defended, protected their homes until the end. They did not have the weapons with which to fight and the main point was the gunpowder factory in Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, we will attempt to prove here that the KLA actually possessed heavy armaments but I wasn't going to go into such questions with you. What I'm asking you is the following: Isn't it obvious that the Serb forces could not advance for three or four days because the KLA engaged in fighting these forces, or is it your view that this person here is simply not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think this witness is in a position to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I agree, Mr. Hannis. The witness has made clear that his knowledge would not allow him to deal with the specific question that's now been asked, Mr. Lukic, and I'm encouraged by my colleagues to take advantage of this opportunity to make it clear to you that we are not in the business of trial by newspaper. A great deal of reference is made to newspaper articles and other trials before this Tribunal. It may be appropriate if an individual who has actually given an interview is faced with a challenge of his evidence from the interview he has given. That would be perhaps a reasonable use of a newspaper. But to use newspaper interviews of other people to cross-examine the witness is unlikely, in our view, to be productive. I appreciate that the rules may allow it in certain circumstances, but it's something we are keen to discourage and -- rather than have the task thrust upon us, of trying to verify the accuracy of newspaper reporting throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll just -- I just have one more question and I think that you'll allow that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salihu, when the Serb forces were advancing towards your village, were you able to observe yourself from the Feronikel factory, that they were held back by KLA fire and they did not manage to advance for three or four days?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: This is a very confusing question. How can you shell from 15 kilometres away and then the KLA be able to attack them? When they were shelling us, we just left. We couldn't fight the army. We just had to flee with our own lives. The army, before entering, before the infantry entered the villages, first the villages were shelled for four or five hours, and then the infantry came in. We had to leave. We couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the part of this article you were referring to starts by saying, "the shelling of the villages around Cicavica started from the Feronikel factory," suggesting that Serb forces were at the Feronikel factory, whereas the question was seemed to be posed on a different basis which might explain why the witness would say this is very confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have in this article somewhere that they were talking that forces were stationed in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's what it sounds like, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I'll move on. I'll abandon this article and try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which would, of course, also explain why NATO would bomb it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously. But in this article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Talks about the cooperation of NATO and KLA but I'll act according to your instructions and leave this aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English page 4, paragraph 2, in the Albanian page 5, paragraph 1, and the B/C/S page 4, paragraph 3, you talk about NATO airplanes circling around the place where you were. At what height were those NATO planes circling around?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said in my statement. When we were taken at the place called Fush e Molles, they took us to a meadow and the Serbs beat us, and after they beat us, they lined us up in two rows, then they asked us to lie down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question has nothing to do with the detail of the events. The question is whether you can help us with the height at which NATO planes were flying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I started to explain the case when the NATO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't need to do that. You just need to tell us how high the planes were. We've got your statement about what was happening in front of us but it doesn't tell us how high the planes were. So that's what we would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were high, flying high, because they looked small. They were quite high up in the sky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How come they were circling at such height? To make a circle at that height it would probably take a plane to go as far as Romania and back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you should ask the people who might know the answer to that question, Mr. Lukic. It's not a question the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is the view of our defence, Mr. Salihu, that the planes could not circle over that area, NATO airplanes, precisely because they were at great height, over 10.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There has been no evidence of this over 10.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they may be flew at 10.000 metres but they had their objectives, their targets down where we were so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you is the following: That it was not possible for NATO aircraft to circle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you can move on, Mr. Lukic. That's not a question for this witness to deal. You've got his evidence about what he claims to have seen and the fact that you think it may not be right or you even think it may be ridiculous is a matter that can be dealt with later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard from you, Mr. Salihu, that you were not a member of the KLA. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No. I wasn't a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know all members of the KLA in the Cicavica area?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Some of them, a few, I would say, because there were not many in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you refer to those 186 [as interpreted] men in the mosque, when you say that they were all civilians --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of them were civilians, all of them were civilians

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I didn't hear your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 176, I believe is his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 176, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's been recorded as 186. Any way could you ask your question again, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, since you do not know who the members of the KLA were, you can not assert that among these 176 men there were no members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No. That's true. Because those who were members of the KLA, they wouldn't be there alive, because if somebody who had a weapon, they would much rather get killed than fall into their hands. So that's why I'm saying it was us civilians, women, children, old people, that we were gathered together. They couldn't catch members of the KLA. All of us were civilians, not members of the KLA, not armed. And that's why I told Milosevic that I regretted not having been a member of the KLA, because I wouldn't have suffered four broken ribs or an injured leg or being beaten like I was. Those who were in the mosque were simple people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also you said to Milosevic, as you had put it at the trial, that at Cicavica, there weren't any KLA fighters and you said that on page 4611.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. I said it then and I say it now. That the population in Cicavica was expelled from Gllogoc to Skenderaj, all the villages, about 20 of them, were expelled. And that went on for two days, 170 people were killed in Cicavica, all of them civilians, a one-month old baby was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, really, I shall have to ask you to try and focus on the questions and please answer the questions. In the area of Cicavica, before these events that you're talking about just now, were there any members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: In the Cicavica area, during the offensive of September 1998, there were no members of the KLA, no army, only expulsion of the population from the whole area, Gllogoc, Skenderaj, people left because of the shelling, went to Cicavica and then we were blocked at the place and we were captured at the place I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it will do if you just give me your position, that is that there were no members of the KLA there. Now we know what your motion is and we can move on. On page 4615 of the Milosevic trial transcript, you say that the KLA was always outside the village. How come that something that is not there at all, that does not exist, is outside the village?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: They were outside the village because if -- if those armed people were there, then the whole population would be killed. There was no fighting there going on. There was only shelling. I mean the September offensive, September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now go back to part of your evidence, when you say that in the area of Cicavica there weren't any members of the KLA? Do you still abide by that position, Mr. Salihu?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Well, do you know what Cicavica is, first of all? Cicavica is a mountain. It's 14 kilometres long and 10 kilometres wide. The expulsions that occurred during the September --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salihu. I just asked you about this Cicavica that you described to us and you explained that it was 14 kilometres long and 10 kilometres wide. Were there any KLA fighters there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No. There were no soldiers there. They were in the villages but not in the Cicavica mountain. There were people who were expelled there in the Cicavica mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Now we have the following position: That members of the KLA and their units are actually in the villages, not in mount Cicavica. Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No. I told you today, and I will say this again, in Prelloc there was a group, the 114 that you mentioned, Baks, Qires, Kresmir Ote [phoen], all the villages around Cicavica had a point altogether and that was not in Cicavica but it was in Prelloc. Cicavica was the place where people went when they were expelled, from Skenderaj and other places. So that army could not mix with the people because if the Serbs had seen an armed person they would kill 100, 200, 300 people on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So these points, they are combat points, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: The points had guard duties because the Serbs sometimes came during the night and we don't call them units, we call them points.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While they were on this guard duty, the members of the Pika [phoen] were in the villages; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: They went to their own homes and then when they had guard duty they went to the place. As I said, the whole villages -- all the villages in that area, they were three or four kilometres away from each other, and they had this organisation, this arrangement. They couldn't fight because they only had some light weapons like Kalashnikovs. They couldn't find the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to take you to page 4616 of the Milosevic transcript. You said to him on this page that you do not know about a single KLA soldier that got killed. Today we heard that you knew of at least two cases when KLA soldiers got killed.
