utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure from reading the transcript whether that's for all time or during the September offensive or which, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salihu, you tell us today about those two persons you mentioned today as being killed, as KLA fighters. Did they actually lose their lives as members of the KLA and when?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: The two I mentioned -- Milosevic did not ask me who was killed and when. His question was, how many soldiers were there in your village? These two were killed on the 30th of April at the Fush e Molles and they were not fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also on page 4618 of the transcript from the Milosevic trial, you said that KLA fighters did not fight. Is that still your position today?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. The same position. It's not true that I've -- I said they did not fight, because they did, but they defended their own homes. You don't need to ask me this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to, Mr. Salihu. And I see that you have changed your position in relation to what you said in the Milosevic trial. What is correct now, in your view? Were the KLA members fighting against the Serb forces or not?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I'm not changing my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have a line from that page that counsel is referring to where he said they did not fight?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which line is it, Mr. Lukic on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 6 on page 4618 from line 6 until line 8, very short part and I can read it. Judge May asked, "Did the KLA at this period, as far as you could see, did they fire any shots? Did you see any firing from the KLA?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "No, fire was not opened."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's my point, Your Honour. That's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, it's quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But -- because in the area he was residing and he was present. He must have seen fire opened against the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a specific question about a specific set of circumstances. I don't think you can draw the conclusion from that that he was saying KLA fighters did not fight. However, you have other evidence from today that you might want to explore on that basis. I don't think it assists you going back to the transcript of the -- that you've identified but that doesn't stop you asking the question you want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salihu, did you personally see KLA fighters opening fire, returning fire, to Serb positions and Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I saw them -- as I said, I knew Sami Lushtaku, you asked me about him earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are not going off on a different journey that you may wish to take us on. We are wanting an answer to the question that's being asked. Have you personal experience of seeing KLA members either opening fire or returning fire to Serb positions? Simple question. We don't need an answer about anyone else. We just need to know about your personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't see any, because we were unarmed, the population was unarmed, so we weren't together with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Amazing how simple these questions can be to answer, you know. Carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you hear from anyone, Mr. Salihu, that there was fighting taking place between the KLA and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Everything that you're saying is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you heard that from somebody else.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I didn't have any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you did not hear from anyone that there was fighting between the KLA and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Well, the Serb forces were shelling at us. There was fighting, of course there was fighting. It would be impossible for there not to have been fighting. But we were the civilian population. We were not able to fight against the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about whether civilians were fighting against the Serb forces. Did you hear of the KLA force fighting against the Serb forces? Did you hear of that? Yes or no? "Yes," if you heard; "no," if you didn't.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you heard about fighting after having gone to Glogovac where they kept you in the cinema and then you heard from people who had come from the ground that there was fighting under way? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I heard about it before we went to Gllogoc, but in -- we were -- had been taken prisoner there. How could I hear anything there? You couldn't speak to the Serbs and ask them because they were beating us all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you in Glogovac, they transferred you to the cinema, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. It was the municipal building beside the cinema, and there was -- the main police station was right there, too, across the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you inside the building?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the corridor of the cinema all day, and at night, they took us down to the basement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: We were told to lie on the floor, on the concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were lying on the floor while you were in that building, right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did the policeman who was guarding you look like? What kind of uniform did he have? What kind of insignia? Can you tell us about that a bit?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: They were normal camouflage uniforms, camouflaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he have a rank?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. He had a rank. I did military service but we had different ranks at that time. They had changed. I didn't know what kind of rank he had but he did have some sort of rank insignia on him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On his shoulder or on his chest?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: On his chest pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he have a cap?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. He had a cap. A type of hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he have a police badge and what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: For a policemen from Gllogoc police station, from the municipality. Everyone knew them there. But -- but I didn't see the colour of their eyes. I couldn't go and take a picture of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that policeman?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Momir Piljevic, he's the one I knew. Momir Piljevic, was the one who interrogated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He interrogated you but who was it that was guarding you? I'm interested in the incident when that man was taken away.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: There are people who know who he was. There were many of -- who knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're lying on the floor and a man with a rifle comes and a bottle of an alcoholic drink and he takes one of you out. As you were lying on the floor, what could you see out of all of this?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Well, some were outside lying on the cement floor and some were inside lying on the cement floor, and I saw it very clearly with my own eyes, how he was shot. And there are other witnesses who saw the incident too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said to us just now that you were inside the building, that you were lying on the floor, and just now you said that you saw with your very own eyes how this man was killed. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: It was possible because I was not only one hour there, I was seven days there, and on the third day, when they took us there, we were on the cement floor but it was outside and they were beating us --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, please, please, just a moment. Are you claiming just now that you were outside the building?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: In the beginning I said that all day we were outside; only in the evening we were put inside. And when the person was killed, Rahman Topilla, he was killed about 10 or 11 in the morning, shot between the eyes. There was concrete floor, both outside and inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to remind you of part of your statement from page 49, line 10. The question was: [In English] "Were you inside the building?" [Interpretation] You answered: [In English] "Yes, it was in the corridor of the cinema, all day. And at night they took us down to the basement." According to this part of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The basement was a mistranslation, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here, according to this part of your evidence, that you were in the corridor in the cinema all day. Now you are claiming to us that you were outside throughout the day all the way up to the evening. One of the two is not true. Which one is not true, Mr. Salihu?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No. What you're saying is not true. I explained very well and I can explain it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not claiming anything, Mr. Salihu. I'm just reading part of your very own statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let the witness now explain, then, to clear it up for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My witness statement is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm looking at page 49 and when he's talking about them being in the basement there is no specific reference to that being at the moment the individual was taken out and killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but the witness now wants to explain the position to us, I think. Carry on, please, Mr. Salihu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They took us to Gllogoc, to that municipality, and it was about 4.00 in the afternoon. They beat us until about 7.00, until the evening. Then they put us inside, into the film auditorium. The floor of the auditorium was cement and the people who were outside, there was cement too. The next day they took us out and they tied us up and started beating us with our hands behinds our heads. All day they held us there and then in the evening they forced us back into the cinema. That's what I said in my statement and I will never forget it. That's the way it was. Rahman Topilla, when he was killed, he was killed at about 10.00 in the morning and we were not inside at that time of day, we were outside. This went on for six or seven days until we went on to Baks, all day, we were outside, until -- until the women told us to go back inside and forced us back in, and they spit at us all the time, and cursed us. Terrible words, they said, and I heard that. I saw that with my own eyes. And what I said in my statement, I experienced that all personally. And if you say, "you were inside, you were outside," I think I explained very clearly that at night we were inside; in the daytime we were outside. It was only in the evening that we were put back into the building and this happened, went on for seven days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, the person who was killed, Topilla, when he was killed, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were all outside. There was no one inside at that time. We were forced out. They were beaten all day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just concentrate on the question, please. When you say outside, where do you mean outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the courtyard of the police station and of the municipal building. There was only a street which separated the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What position -- what position were you in when he was actually killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were sitting down on the floor in a circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something, Mr. Salihu, something pertaining to yourself. Have you ever been convicted in a trial proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In a criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was one case. Not for anything to do with the KLA or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the exact spelling of your name?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: My name is Abdullah Salihu.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When one of the officers of this Court made the attestation, and he probably referred to your official document, we realised that your name was not spelled the same way as it was on the statements. There are even differences between what was written in the Albanian version and in the B/C/S and the English versions on the other side. As regards the attestation, your name is spelled A-v-d-u-l-l-a Salihu. Is this the correct spelling of your first name? Your first name is actually Avdulla and not Abdullah?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: It's not Avdulla; it's Abdullah. And in all my papers my ID, I have it as A-b-d, et cetera. Abdullah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your father's name is Nebih; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were born on the 17th of January. What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By a judgement by the municipal court in Pristina, were you convicted on the 24th of March 1971 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, I said so. I don't know, don't remember the date any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you also convicted by a district court in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interject here. May I inquire whether these documents have been disclosed to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The documents haven't been disclosed because we don't have any. We just inquired and we don't have the documents yet. We don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I'm concerned about the good faith basis for asking this question if we don't have these documents in hand. If they refer to convictions in 1971 when he would have been 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise, that's what I heard. It's in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He would have been a juvenile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked about 81. I apologise. I didn't check the transcript. Can the witness answer, Your Honour? Or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've got an answer. The answer was, "No, I wasn't." So the matter has been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1997, was a criminal report submitted against you based on the law on ammunition and firearms? And was any -- were any weapons seized from you back in 1997?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let us have an answer to the first part of that question, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And again, may I inquire whether or not we have that document, that it's been disclosed to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have the document, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I just have an inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You must have a basis for asking there question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do have a basis but I don't have a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he doesn't have a document then I don't know who he's got the information from and I have a concern about this. Those kind of questions being asked without a better basis for the question ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking this witness. He knows if the weapon is confiscated. He knows about the event. That's -- I'm asking him. If he does not know about the criminal proceeding, he has to know about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why don't you just go directly to the question, then? Let's have that, whether any weapons were seized from him in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't mention any document. I just asked the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You did. You said, "In 1997, was a criminal report submitted against you?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does he know? Is he aware of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now that's a document, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, but I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you also say you didn't mention it. Now let's be frank about it, Mr. Lukic. That's where you start, and you don't have the document. What you actually want to know is whether he's ever had a weapon seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, can he ask that question, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my concern is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know what your concern is but what's wrong with that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, because it borders on the, "Isn't it true you still beat your wife," when all he may have heard is somebody say, "So and so beats his wife." If there's a document, then he should have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I repel that objection. You may ask the question and whether a weapon was confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, in 1996 or 1997, were there any weapons seized from you?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions and I would like to thank you for your answers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As a matter of fact, with a view of the cross-examination that had already been conducted, all I have are three to four questions and, by your leave, I wanted to ask them of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, I'm an attorney at law, one of the counsel for General Vladimir Lazarevic. In your statement and in your testimony today you mentioned the September offensive in 1998 at Mount Cicavica. Did you know that the Serb forces at that time arrested 420 KLA members, out of which most have been instigated, proceedings against?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear about that. I don't know how many were arrested. I would think about 40 people were arrested and they were released too late -- two days later in Gllogoc. They beat them up and let them go two days ago, two days later. About 80 people killed. But about 400 KLA, I don't have information on that. I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salihu.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Could I add something, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, just wait for the next question, please, Mr. Salihu. Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, in your statement, on page 5 in the English, the third paragraph on page 6, the first paragraph of the Albanian, you stated, the next morning, the 30th of April 1999, four military jeeps arrived before the mosque, three were of green colour and there was a white Land Rover as well. My question is whether there were any markings on those jeeps.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No, they didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that the white one was a Land Rover. As for the other three, what brand, what make were there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I just know that they were army vehicles. I don't know -- and the white one didn't have any licence plate or sign on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, if those three jeeps had no markings, and since you don't know what make of jeep they were, how could you tell that these were military jeeps?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. Military jeeps had registries on them. That was clear. I was in the army. I know what the registries are, with a J, with an N, and the numbers. I couldn't read the numbers, so I can't give you exact information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salihu. In the continuation of the same paragraph, you say that the Serb officer who commanded had long, black hair, and his major feature was that he had only one tooth in his upper jaw. He was skinny, 192 centimetres tall, of dark complexion, black eyes, and had a red scarf over his head. Wouldn't this description tally with a description of a paramilitary, for example, as you had already said before?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: More or less, I would think so. He was a paramilitary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salihu.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Salihu, when Mr. Ackerman was asking you a question about your statement in the Milosevic testimony about your regret in not joining the KLA. At page 24 line 10 of today's transcript, you said you would like to explain something. Do you recall what that was and do you want to do that now?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I wanted to say that if I'd been a member of the KLA, I would not have been captured like that because they didn't capture any members of the KLA alive, and to save myself, I would have been in a better position now, if I had been a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. One other question I had for you. Mr. Bakrac, who just finished asking you a few questions, asked you about whether you knew about the 420 KLA arrested after the Cicavica offensive, and after answering that question you asked if you could add something, please. Was there something you wanted to add to that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No. It was just that I hadn't understood the question as being in relation to my statement. I have said that about 170 or 180 were killed and 40 or 50 were taken over a period of two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Judge Chowhan has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you, were you an imam of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: I started working at the mosque in 2001 or - sorry - 2003, because in 2001 we built the mosque and I started serving there in 2003. I worked in the month of Ramadan, and I worked in Jashanica - that is a village near Klina - for a year, about a year. And now I work in the mosque there in that village, in my village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: What sort of work are you doing with the mosque?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Well, there are special Islamic rites that we deal with, once a week on Fridays, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Can you elucidate? Can you tell what you're doing in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: We pray in the mosque, five times a day, and then we return home, we are free after prayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the work you're doing in the mosque. Are you a muezzin or are you doing some other things?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: No, I'm an imam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You lead the prayers?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. I lead the prayers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: My next question would be what happened to Mirsad for whom they came looking in the village, Mirsad.

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: The police captured us and took us to Qires and there, there was a photograph of a Bosnian, a man from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Is he the man called Mirsad? Was he named Mirsad?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: The police had the photograph in their hands and they said, this is a person called Mirsad and he must be returned to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: He was not caught, then, no?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: But that wasn't the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I see. What happened to those nine persons who were members of the KLA in your village? Did you find out about them later on? Two you said were killed but what happened to the rest?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: They are still alive today and are at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You mean the seven of them?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Did you have your medical examination for the ribs and the leg which were broken, as you allege?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Do you still have the scars? You still have the signs of those injuries?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Both on the chest and the leg?

utterances.speaker: ABDULLAH SALIHU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give evidence, and you are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for listening to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, is the next witness Emin Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could take him after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would request that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We would resume at quarter to 1.00. I wonder if with this witness and any other -- well, all others, you would please direct our attention to the paragraphs of the indictment that the witness is speaking to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you like us to do that at the beginning, before the witness comes on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be helpful if you were able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's been quite difficult with this last witness to try to relate his evidence to the indictment. And we would be assisted therefore by guidance in advance of the witness's giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that regard, Your Honour, I can tell you the next witness, Mr. Kabashi speaks to 72(G) and 72(G)(i).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. 72(G). I would call that one but I think it's a Roman, it's a small Roman numeral rather than a letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I may have misread the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It gets complicated, actually, if you do refer to it as a letter rather than a number. It may sound trivial but it can begin to become complicated. All right. Thank you very much. Well, the witness should be in place when we resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the paper which will now be placed in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Now, Mr. Kabashi, we have a full statement of your account of events and we also have the written record of evidence which you gave when you came to the Tribunal before, so we already have a lot of information about what you can tell us. The purpose of today is for counsel to explore matters that they wish to ask you further questions about, whether to expand what you've said or perhaps to challenge what you've said. And don't be surprised if you're challenged because that's part of the exercise that takes place under the system we operate in this Tribunal. The first of the counsel to ask questions will be on behalf of the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are proceeding with this witness as a 92 bis witness and the transcript is Exhibit P2251 and his statement that was tendered as part of his testimony is P2250. We would tender those at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's noted, Mr. Hannis, and you regard him as giving evidence under paragraph (D) of 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kabashi. I want to confirm a few things --

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- that are in your written statement. Sir, can you tell us what your title is? I understand you have a Ph.D. in Philology. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I am a doctor of philological sciences. I got my degree from the University of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, before you came to testify today, did you have a chance last week to meet with representatives from the OTP to go through your written statement and note any changes or corrections that you felt needed to be made?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes. But there was no need to make any correction or changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Other than a few minor things that were discussed which I'll ask you about shortly I wanted to start by asking you your statement starts with the 25th of March 1999, a day after the NATO bombing started, when you described a bomb being thrown into your own home on the 25th of March. Your home was located where?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: My house was and still is, after being repaired, so it is in the Fushe Kosova town. It is in the northwestern part of Pristina, about seven kilometres from Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is the Serbian name for that town Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that before the bomb was thrown in your house, you received an anonymous call. Can you tell us any details about the call you received before the bomb was thrown?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: That day, I had gone to my home because of my mother's ill health. Nobody was there to take care of her, and during the time I was at home, while I was caring for her, I had several phone calls. Nobody spoke at the other end of the line but on one of those calls, somebody spoke to me in Serbian and said, "You people who are waiting for NATO, you will be killed, you have to go to Albania and such things".

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you speak and understand the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you detailed that event in your statement. And I want to go to page 3 of the English version, the first paragraph. You mention that that night you heard that there were 44 people killed in your neighbourhood. What was the ethnicity of those people who were killed on the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: My neighbourhood was mainly inhabited by Albanians and all the killed people were Albanians. Among them were old people, women, children. Some of them I knew personally because they were my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what percentage of non-Albanians lived in that part of town, in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In my neighbourhood, 80 per cent or even 85 per cent of the inhabitants were Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you describe how after that event you went to stay with a neighbour and then you went to Pristina, and you and your group went to the Dragodan neighbourhood of Pristina. I'd like to show you a map, if we could put up Exhibit P13. Mr. Kabashi, Dr. Kabashi, you should see on your screen in a moment a map. I want to know if you recognise what's depicted there. I don't know if we need to blow that up a little bit. Perhaps I should say enlarge. Can we take it down a little bit?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes. This is a map of Pristina. It has to go a little bit down in order to be -- to be able to see Dragodan, even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's the end of our map for Pristina.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: If you could go a little lower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if Dragodan appears on this particular map.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. Dragodan is not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If the bottom of the page is south, in what direction would Dragodan be from this map?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Dragodan should be in the direction of the north, between Lakrishta, the neighbourhood, and Lahja e Ymerajve [phoen] neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we move toward the top of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this map were to be taken down to the bottom, I think it does have the actual name there, if I understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We can move now to the top of the map. I think --

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, now I can see it. Yes. Here is Dragodan here. This is hilly neighbourhood of Pristina. It was built after the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you stayed there for, I think you said, three days before the army and the special police came and broke in the front door. Can you explain to us what you mean by the term "special police"? In terms of uniform, appearance, equipment, how would you distinguish them from regular police?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They were together with the army, but the door was broken by the police, the special police. They were different in uniform, armament, the masks they were wearing, painted faces. This was the -- how they were different from the normal police that we had seen at other times in Fushe Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you describe in what way the uniforms were different, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The uniforms were darker than the normal police uniforms. They also had painted faces, some wore masks. The other ones who did not have masks had painted faces. We were not able to recognise them because of that. Some of them had automatic guns and knives, and they were wearing also baseball caps or caps that were similar to baseball caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did the --

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: And we knew that these were the special Serbian police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did any of those men wear any insignia or ranking or badges on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the ranks. I did not observe them very closely. But they had on their sleeves, they had the police insignia, as opposed to the army, that the soldiers had army insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say the army, are you referring to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you describe their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It was lighter in colour, lighter than the police uniform, and it was camouflage, so more patches on the uniform. They were not masked. And on the left side, they had this insignia, this thing that wrote, "soldier of the Yugoslav army."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, before these police and soldiers came to the place where you were staying in Dragodan, during those three days, did you have a chance to observe what was happening around that part of town in the Dragodan suburb of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Although I was in Dragodan for those three days and three nights, in fact, it was three nights and two days because in the morning we were taken out of that place. I moved about a little bit. I knew the terrain, the area. I saw that the people were being expelled from their own homes. I saw that the house of a very well known doctor in Pristina had been bombed. I saw intellectuals who had left their homes and gone elsewhere, professors, doctors, people like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see how the people were being expelled and by whom?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Usually the people were expelled by the police, but in Dragodan, the army was there too. They went into certain neighbourhoods, they surrounded it, and then went into the homes where there were still people living there. They told them to go out into the street and showed them the direction where to go. This was normally what happened. This was the procedure that was followed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see any other uniformed men moving around Pristina other than the army and the special police that you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not only in Pristina but also in Fushe Kosova and other parts of Pristina, including Dragodan. We've seen -- we saw during those days other kinds of uniforms and other kinds of people who were armed, who, according to the information we had, including the Serbian press and television. So we knew from those that these were Arkan's men, Frenki Simatovic's men, and so on. These were different from the other formations, also because of their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you see any of those yourself, and in what way were they different from the other formations?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I did not see just one or two. I saw several formations, several units, I would say. They had darker uniforms. On their heads they wore caps differently from the Frenki's men who had berets with a red ribbon around their berets. And their armament, their weapons, were different from the normal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In what way were the weapons different, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They mainly had automatic guns, probably Kalashnikovs, sniper rifles, with a telescopic sights.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you indicate that after the men came and took you out of the house in Dragodan, that you went elsewhere and were taken in for a while. How long did you stay at that second location? I believe you say in your statement it was with the family of Qamil Berisha.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, after seven years, it must have been one night. The next day, by mid-day, we were told to leave. We went to the -- to a house in the same neighbourhood, in Ajazi's house - he was a correspondent of -- a reporter for Radio Pristina - and the next morning, the police and the army came and took us out of there, after the fighting that had happened in this part of the neighbourhood where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where did the police take you or send you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The police had told all the inhabitants of the neighbourhood to go to the main street, to the centre of Pristina. This is the neighbourhood called Kodra e Diellit in Albanian or Venrac [phoen]. From that neighbourhood we were told to go down to the main road. On the left it's the Madrasah, the Islamic seminar, and on the right it's the train station. In Venrac over the railroad there is a bridge where I could see a tank on that day and the convoy I was part of was divided into two by the -- by an order released from that -- issued from that tank. My part of the convoy was told to go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then we see in your statement that you eventually made your way to the train station after a few --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you one question about that, Mr. Kabashi? Which train station was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Pristina train station. Pristina has got only one train station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there also a train station at Fushe Kosova?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Fushe Kosova train station is an international line. The international trains pass there, while the Pristina train station, it's before you get to Fushe Kosova to -- so from Pristina to Fushe Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You describe in your statement how eventually you were put on the train and made your way with all the other people that were being forced out to the border with Macedonia where you had to get off the train and walk across the border; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it happened. Well, you can say things in two sentences but what happened there and what we experienced there, the horror of the displacement, of the expulsion, of leaving your own country, is something that you can just not express in two sentences. But it was like what you -- like you said. After two or three days, that we had stayed at the station, I was in the last group that got on a freight train. We were sent towards Hani i Elezit they told to us get off there and walk along the line, along the tracks, because if we went outside the tracks, the terrain was mined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Rest assured, Mr. Kabashi, we have a very full account of what you have to say on these matters, as well as the written record of the evidence you gave before. So there is no question of a couple of sentences simply being used to try to explain your whole evidence. Thank you. Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand your point, Dr. Kabashi. You understand the Judges do have your written statement and your prior testimony and I'm just trying to move quickly through that because they do have more details. I did not mean to denigrate your experience in any way. You also, in your statement, you make a statement about the NATO bombing. You say the NATO bombing did not affect residential areas in Pristina. How were you able to observe that or come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It's not that I came to certain conclusions. I did not make a certain analysis. I can only tell you about the things that I saw in Pristina. The only building that was damaged in Pristina was the police station, and that happened during the second night, when I was in Dragodan, and as the crow flies, I was only 500 metres from the police station and I could see and I could hear the people's voices, mainly the policemen's voices that were withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In the whole of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you start to say something?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I was saying that in the city of Pristina, the whole of the city, and this was -- excuse me -- where there were no military buildings, the only thing that was bombed was the Pristina police station and the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement, there is a reference to the courthouse being bombed as well. Is that part of the police station or the prison?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They are next to each other. Even after the renovation, the reconstruction, of this building, they are still together, the courthouse, the prison, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you describe in your statement, on page 5 of the English, at the last paragraph, the chaos that was at the train station when you were there for three days and three nights. You mention that there were so many people being forced on the trains that some people died in the crush. How do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I saw them with my own eyes, because I was one of the, if I can call myself, spectators of this drama happening there. People were forced to get on the trains so that wouldn't be killed and beaten, and there was such chaos, the people crushed each other. Sometimes they got run over by the train. So I have seen with my own eyes how, after the train got on its way, people were run over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During that time you mentioned that between five and 12 trains were leaving each day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I counted them during those days I stayed there. I couldn't count all the buses but I counted all the trains, because I was in the last group of people that was forced to leave Pristina, and every day there were five to 12 trains with lots of cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you able to give us any rough estimate of the numbers of people that were shipped out on the trains during those three days? Are we talking about hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Well, this is not a matter of hundreds of thousands -- hundreds or thousands. It's tens of thousands of people who were expelled from Pristina during those three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And among the people being put on the trains and the people that you met when you crossed the border and went to the refugee camp that you told us about, were there any Serbs in that group or on the trains? Or was it only Albanians, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I remember the event well, even today, because I still experience it. No, I didn't meet any Serbs among the people, and I was very surprised, when I met three gypsies in Bllaca. They were the only three people and I still can't understand why they were there with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no more questions for Dr. Kabashi at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions for this witness. We will proceed in the following order: General Pavkovic, Mr. Sainovic, General Lazarevic, General Lukic, and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, my name is John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic in this proceeding. I have some questions to ask you that I hope will be easy for you to answer simply and briefly. If you can do that we will get through this rather quickly. If not, then it's going to take us much longer. And so I'm depending on your cooperation. Can I count on that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It depends on the level of cooperation you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think that answer makes a lot of sense. I agree with you. Let me start with that period right after you say that your home was attacked. You went to Pristina and you stayed at the home of a Qemal Avdiu, and this was in the Dragodan area of Pristina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Dragodan area of Pristina, as you have told us earlier today and showed us on a map, is an area that's located on the edge of Pristina, up on a hill, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes. It's at the edge of town at the northwestern side, and it's very -- it was very populated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you said in your statement that it was an area from which you were able to view the town of Pristina pretty easily.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is there an oil storage facility of some kind located in the Dragodan area, on that hill?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: At the time there wasn't near that area. Before you enter the Dragodan area you cross a bridge and then you turn left, and near the bridge there, on the right side, there was a gas station but it was not really part of the Dragodan neighbourhood. It was called the hospital neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, do you know of any oil storage facility in the Dragodan area that was bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You had been at the home of this Qemal Avdiu for about three days when you claim that the army and the special police broke in the front door of the house. I want to know how many army and police there were who did that.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In the house where I was staying, there were eight policemen and four soldiers. I counted them myself because I had time, and on the two sides of the road, in that neighbourhood where we were expelled, the direction we were expelled, there were dozens more. I can't tell you exactly how many there were but I would think 40 or 50 in all on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about the four soldiers that you say you saw there. I think you've said that they were wearing blue camouflage uniforms, light blue camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how old would you say they were? Their ages, what would you say, their ages, these four?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They could have been from, say, 22 to 27 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Any of them have beards or long hair, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not the soldiers, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Any scarves or arm bands?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They did have helmets, but I didn't see any scarves around their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You must know, don't you, that the VJ doesn't have any blue uniforms, light blue uniforms. Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that they had blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, page 4 of your statement in English, at least, near the top, what you said was, "the soldiers wore blue camouflage uniforms which were lighter than the police uniforms." So according to the information I've been furnished about your statement, which you swore to, you did say that they were wearing blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They were camouflage uniform, and because of the camouflage, they seemed lighter than the normal police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said "blue." Do you now contest they were not blue? That's what I want to know now.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. I don't contest that. But it wasn't the same blue as the police uniforms. They were camouflage and they had different insignia and the whole uniform was different. And it seemed to be of a lighter colour than the normal blue of the other uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, again I'll ask you: You know, don't you, that the VJ does not wear light blue uniforms, light blue camouflage uniforms, those are not VJ uniforms, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They told us themselves that they were soldiers, they said, "We are soldiers," and they had on their shoulders, they had the insignia of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, do you know that paramilitary groups used to wear insignia of the Yugoslav army just to confuse people? Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I've read and heard about that but I have never met any such groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you may have without knowing it. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go now to the time you went to the railway station. You say on page 4 in the English of your statement that you -- at the railway station you saw a list that had been compiled on a computer. So you actually saw a computer screen with a list on it? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. There were no computer screens in the road at that time. But a policeman took out of his pocket a list which had been printed on a -- by a computer, but an English-language computer programme with a large "I" on it, which wasn't either Albanian or Serbian, and there was a list of names on the list. That was before we went to the train station, when we were in the column. The police had check-points from time to time and would ask people things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this police officer showed you this list?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They asked us about the names and then I saw the list and I saw the names on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, did he show you the list? Did he hand you a list and say, "Look at this list"? Did you get it from him and look at it? What happened? How did you happen to see your name on it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I saw it. It was in his hand and I was standing right beside him. The officer had stopped us, or a policeman had stopped us rather, and the other policemen had this list of names and was asking about people's names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were looking over his shoulder, standing next to him, looking at the list, is that -- is that how that happened?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Must have been a pretty friendly policeman to stand there next to you and let you look at the list. Would you say that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. I wasn't behind his back, if you mean that. I was beside him, standing beside him. I don't know what sort of fellow he was, but the fact that he let us pass alive means that he was a nice guy, and I'm talking about pure survival here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have no idea what that list was for or what it meant, do you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I know. It's not only that I have a speculation but I know exactly what it was. In Pristina and in other towns at that time, people were being sought, and if they were caught, they were either killed or imprisoned at the time. And in the group of names on the list, I saw the names of several people I knew and my name was on the list too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did it say "liquidation list" or something like that at the top? Is that how you knew what it was?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. I didn't read the title at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So maybe you just sort of guessed that that's what that list was about, that it was some kind of a list where they were trying to capture you specifically.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Well, I knew that because there were many such cases in Pristina. People were being sent away to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: If they got caught.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're guessing that based on the fact that there were many such cases in Pristina, not upon actual knowledge. Isn't that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I suppose you could say that if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, and I suppose you'd agree with me, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: At that time, it wasn't a question of whether I wanted or didn't want. Convictions were made on -- personal convictions were made on the basis of what was happening. People were being arrested. They were being killed. They were being sent away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many. I think three times before this moment, you claim that doors of houses you were in were broken down and you were thrown out of those houses, and if they were looking for you it seems to me on those three occasions they found you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes. On two cases -- two cases, not the third. On two occasions the police talked to me and on -- the third case was the case where I saw the list of names at the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go forward here. On your -- in your statement, page 6 in the English version, at least, you say that the -- talking about Kosovo and leaving Kosovo and things of that nature. You say the population was totally undefended, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If a witness has told us that the KLA was defending the people, was that wrong? Were they not being defended by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not the columns of people. They were certainly not being defended. The columns of people weren't-- no one was defending them. Those who were protected by the KLA were in other areas of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's try to be a little more precise, then, about this issue. If I look at the part of the statement that I was referring to, it appears to me that you're talking in general terms about Kosovo. You say this: "I did not want to leave Kosovo. We left because we were forced by the actions and words of the Serb police and army to leave. As a family we were not organised to fight. I do not know who can stay in Kosovo when threatened by guns." Now, you're not talking about large columns of people; you're talking about the general population. And that's when you say the population was totally undefended. Now, they either were totally undefended or they were defended by the KLA as we've been told by another witness, and I just want to know which of those you think is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's argumentative. He said, I left, we all left as a family we were not organised to fight. I don't think it's clear from reading that, that it refers to the entire population of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's also clear from the previous answer that the witness accepts that the KLA were present in Kosovo. So, Mr. Ackerman, it's difficult it see what's to be achieved by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were a member of the KLA, were you not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know how many members there were of the KLA at its highest point? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, I don't. I have -- I was never interested in those such statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you testified in the Milosevic case, and I'm at page 4018, you told the Trial Chamber there that you became a member of the KLA because, "I saw that the only way for our people to win their freedom was by means of the gun." That was your testimony, was it not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes. But the thought expressed is exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you also said that from 1997 when you joined the KLA, you prepared a lot of literature, and, as you said, you made every effort to explain to others that the only -- only the path of war can bring us freedom. True?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes. The -- what I said to others may not be totally valid but I did say that to the students in the few years I was allowed to be a teacher. And this was the main reason, and that's what I said to my students. That was the reason I gave for having joined the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you think you may have inspired a number of your students to take up arms and make that war against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I think that all the soldiers I met were probably my students. I know them from that age group. Most of them were my students.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I guess you were successful in your quest to make that point. And the purpose of the KLA then in your view was to make war against the Serbs and win freedom for Kosovo Albanians by force of arms, by the gun. Right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not against the Serbs. Against the occupants, the occupiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who were the occupiers if they weren't Serbs? Was it the gypsies and the -- those people or who are you going to make war against?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: What I mean is the Serb government, the state and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I accept that clarification. I want to go back now to the attack on your home, back at the beginning. You say a bomb was thrown at your home. And you say it was done by police and by local residents, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And were you able to see the people who threw this bomb at your home before they threw the bomb?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. I didn't see them before they threw the bomb. If I had seen them, I would have done something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you must agree that it's fair to say that you don't know who threw the bomb at your home if you didn't see them before.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. I'd have to make an explanation here. I did not see them before they threw the bomb but I did see them after they threw the bomb because my house is constructed in such a way that I can see the road from various positions. You can see the road where the people are leaving the house, getting away from the house. And aside from that, I heard the voices of people whom I knew because they had been my neighbours for a long time. And on top of that, I knew people who worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you're saying it could have been one of your neighbours who threw the bomb at your house?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not one of my neighbours. Several, two or three. I don't know which one of them threw the bomb because they were all around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You then said - this is at page 4039 of the Milosevic transcript and your testimony there - that after they had thrown the bomb they then shot at the window. And then you say this: "Thinking that I or someone else from my family will be standing." Now there is no way you would know what they were thinking, is there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact wording as to which of us would have been standing but I do remember the events and I've described them and I can repeat them, if you wish. I was in the corridor --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't need to repeat them because the Judges can read them. What I'm trying to -- I think you didn't mean to tell the Milosevic Trial Chamber that you knew what the people outside were thinking. Am I right about that? Or did you know what they were thinking?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They knew that I was a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ackerman, this may be another example of what inferences a person might start to draw from the circumstances against their own background knowledge. In any event, you'll see the time and my question is, is this a convenient moment to interrupt until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume we can't go further, so it probably is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unless, if you wanted to complete something then you can do that but otherwise we are stuck with the stop watch, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, I have ten questions that will probably take more than 10 or 15 minutes so I think probably stopping is the thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could I inquire of the Defence team, an estimate on their remaining time for cross in this witness for planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there someone in the position to answer that question with overall knowledge of how long the Defence cross-examination will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We can meet with Mr. Hannis when we break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Kabashi we have to break there for the day because another case occupies the afternoon here so we have to adjourn until tomorrow. And in our case we will be here in the afternoon tomorrow. So we break now until 2.15 tomorrow. You need to come back ready to resume giving evidence at 2.15 tomorrow. Meanwhile, it's vital that you should not discuss your evidence with anyone at all, and that refers to both the evidence you have already given and any evidence you may yet give in the case. You can talk about anything else with anybody you meet, except the evidence in this case. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I read that in the regulations of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will see you again tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of August, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
